records.label: Bactra/Balkh oasis archaeological feeding-capacity reconstruction
records.interval_semantics: Physical feeding-capacity interval, not a census: 2700 km2 irrigated area combined with traditional-cultivar densities and alternative fallow cycles gives approximately 300k, 325k, or 400k people.
pressure_evidence: de la Vaissière (2017, pp. 802–805) reconstructs the early-medieval Bactra oasis from hundreds of archaeological sites and an oasis wall; 300 km2 of the approximately 3000 km2 oasis were deserts/swamps and 2700 km2 were irrigated.
The paper documents abandoned and poorly irrigated villages after the Mongol destruction and distinguishes annual irrigation from fallow lands, making water and land-use constraints explicit.

Independent traditional-agriculture data give 2.1 people/ha on annual irrigation and lower densities for biennial-to-quadrennial fallow; the resulting capacity range is calculated in the cited paper, not fitted to EU5 populations.
shock_flags: Capacity is reconstructed from archaeological area plus ethnographic productivity, not a 1337 equilibrium observation
Mongol-era irrigation destruction is a later shock relative to the reconstruction
Local-food share and imports are not resolved
records.food_regime: irrigated cereals, gardens and livestock in a Central Asian oasis
records.boundary_description: Early-medieval Bactra/Balkh oasis bounded by archaeological sites, channels and a preserved oasis wall; not equivalent to the EU5 Balkh location polygon.
records.notes: High-value physical validation analogue with an explicit capacity calculation. It is blocked for scale fitting because its date is out of period, population/local-food saturation is unresolved, and the archaeological oasis cannot be overlaid to >=95% of the EU5 Balkh province selector.

records.label: Bukhara oasis early-medieval feeding-capacity range
records.interval_semantics: Physical capacity scenarios from a roughly 3200 km2 oasis: approximately 360k under a Bactra-like land-use mix and up to 690k if all land were annually irrigated; these are not a population census.
pressure_evidence: de la Vaissière (2017, pp. 806–808) maps the approximately 3200 km2 Bukhara oasis wall and reconstructs its irrigation network from Arabic geographic descriptions.

The article reports more water than needed in the oasis, dense gardens and no barren track in 10th-century descriptions, but also notes that grain could be sent downstream from the Zarafshan valley; the upper interval is therefore not a local-food saturation label.

The cited analysis gives a 360k–690k physical feeding range and separately treats the likely Samanid population as closer to the upper end, preserving capacity and observed population as distinct quantities.
shock_flags: Observed population likely included grain transfers from the Zarafshan valley
Irrigation-network reconstruction is approximate and the Qaraqul extension is hypothetical
No independent saturation fraction or local-food share
records.food_regime: irrigated cereals, gardens, orchards and livestock; downstream grain transfers documented
records.boundary_description: Early-medieval Bukhara oasis inside a partially preserved 12×12 farsakh wall plus uncertain Paykent/Qaraqul fringes; not equivalent to the EU5 Bukhara location polygon.
records.notes: Useful irrigated-oasis capacity stress test, but explicitly validation-only because date, imported grain and archaeological-to-EU5 boundary uncertainty violate the scale-anchor contract.

records.label: Middle Zarafshan valley irrigated and rainfed capacity reconstruction
records.interval_semantics: Physical capacity scenario from approximately 3500 km2 irrigated land plus roughly 1800 km2 rainfed land; the paper's 580k–800k range is a hypothesis about feeding power, not an enumerated population interval.
pressure_evidence: de la Vaissière (2017, pp. 808–811) reconstructs the Bulungur, Dargom and Yangi Ariq channels and an approximately 3500 km2 irrigated middle Zarafshan zone from archaeological settlements and geographic texts.

The paper models annual irrigation, fallow cycles and rainfed contributions, then checks the result against 1897 census densities and concludes a middle hypothesis around 580k–600k observed people for the valley.

The capacity calculation is explicitly marked as a maximum/technical possibility during high-water periods, so it is retained as a held-out physical validation case rather than a 1337 saturation anchor.
shock_flags: Potential high-water and channel-use assumptions are scenario bounds, not observed equilibrium
Valley spans multiple historical and EU5 administrative units
No local-food share; inter-oasis grain exchange is possible
records.food_regime: irrigated wheat, gardens, dairy and extensive rainfed agriculture
records.boundary_description: Middle Zarafshan valley from Waraghsar to the Bukhara-fan entrance, including irrigated and rainfed zones; not equivalent to the EU5 Samarkand province selector.
records.notes: Strong mechanistic benchmark for irrigation, fallow and rainfed allocation. It cannot supervise 1337 scale because it is out of period and its valley boundary has no audited >=95% EU5 overlay.
